A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SMD research, with matching authors, methods and original benchmarks. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original multi-robot planning experiments, including success rates, path lengths, acceleration and collisions in Sections 5–6 and Appendix B.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds runtime measurements, evaluations on additional maps and penalty-scaling sensitivity results in Appendix C.

M1.justification: Algorithm 2 replaces one shared stopping tolerance with separate robot-collision and obstacle-collision tolerances, a small procedural generalization. The diffusion model, projection constraints and augmented-Lagrangian procedure remain. Specifying multiplicative penalty updates mainly adds implementation detail.

E1.justification: Table 6 adds evaluation on the prior MMD work's Highways, Conveyor and Drop-Region map families beyond the original six map types. This substantially extends evaluated environment coverage while retaining planar multi-robot planning and the 3, 6 and 9 robot configurations.

E2.justification: DM, MPD, MMD and EECBS remain in the corresponding original comparisons. The added runtime comparison reuses existing learning baselines, and the additional maps compare SMD with the existing MMD baseline. Shaoul's publication-year update does not introduce another method.

E3.justification: v2 adds runtime evaluation with failed MMD generations excluded from timing, plus a controlled six-value penalty-scaling study. The original 4,000-instance evaluation, robot counts, performance metrics and Appendix A training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Figures 9–10 introduce systematic sensitivity and ablation experiments absent from v1. They compare constant penalty scaling with five increasing factors and track inter-robot and obstacle-constraint gradient convergence across map types and robot counts, directly testing the projection solver's behavior.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests. The new convergence plots distinguish parameter settings rather than reporting uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 5–6 add runtimes and additional-map results; both MMD and SMD achieve 100% success and zero collisions in every Table 6 configuration. Figures 9–10 add convergence findings. Original Table 3 results remain unchanged, while Table 4 changes EECBS corridor success from 0.7120 to 1.

T1.justification: v2 adds Assumption 4.1, Proposition 4.2, Remark 4.3 and an Appendix B proof concerning convex feasibility and nonconvex residual tolerances. It also replaces v1's explicit Langevin convergence-rate expression with a noise/step-size approximation statement and corrects feasible-set and obstacle-index definitions.

C1.justification: Contribution 3 shifts from improving the frequency of satisfying nonconvex constraints to claiming improved efficiency supported theoretically and empirically. The central claims about constrained diffusion, feasible multi-robot trajectories and the benchmark remain substantially unchanged.

C2.justification: Appendix C newly interprets the sensitivity results as requiring little tuning and the additional maps as supporting practical reliability. Section 6.1 strengthens the interpretation to exclusive feasibility in the largest complex settings, although Table 3 retains nonzero MMD and EECBS successes. The conclusion also identifies new future applicability directions.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link, specifies multiplicative penalty scaling and recommends a moderate factor of 1.05. It removes v1's disclosure of feasibility checking and regeneration during task assignment, without establishing that this procedure actually changed. Hardware, software and training hyperparameters are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Kotary and Fioretto (2024), Naderiparizi et al. (2025), and Xu et al. (2018) for optimization, constrained generation and convergence context. The broader positioning remains intact; updates to existing works' publication details are not new citations.

P1.justification: The revision makes targeted wording and terminology changes, subdivides Section 4, inserts a proof appendix and moves the existing experimental appendix from B to C. It also adds acknowledgments and revises future-work prose, while preserving most of the original narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds two tables and two extensive multipanel convergence figures. It redraws Figure 1 with explicit infeasibility markings, updates trajectory illustrations, corrects the corridor caption and relocates existing displays. These substantially expand the visual presentation beyond numerical table updates.

improvement.justification: The runtime measurements, additional-map evaluations, sensitivity experiments and code-access information improve empirical scrutiny and reproducibility beyond v1. These benefits are tempered by weaknesses in the additions: Appendix B infers uniqueness from convexity alone, and Section 6.1's exclusive-feasibility claim conflicts with retained baseline successes. The empirical transparency improves, but the added theory and stronger claims do not establish a substantial overall quality gain.
